say: I'm afraid the proposal, ingenious as it is, simply doesn't hold water.
q: What does the speaker think of the proposal?
options: clever but logically flawed
brilliant and completely sound
dull but basically correct
affordable but badly presented

say: Not once in all my years at the library have I seen a book return itself.
options: He has never seen it happen.
He sees it happen about once a year.
He saw it happen only once, long ago.
He works at a bookshop, not a library.

say: He's been resting on his laurels ever since that first prize.
options: He relies on past success and doesn't try.
He is too tired to compete after winning.
He has won far too many prizes to count.
He spends all his free time growing plants.

say: Were I in your shoes, I'd think twice before signing.
options: Be cautious about signing.
Sign the contract immediately.
Buy a new pair of shoes first.
Sign two copies, just in case.
explain: Were I in your shoes = If I were you.

say: That's rather a moot point now that the funding's been withdrawn.
options: The question is no longer relevant.
The point is now more important than ever.
They should keep arguing about it at length.
The funding has been increased, not cut.
explain: Here 'moot' = no longer of practical importance.

say: She's not one to suffer fools gladly.
options: impatient with foolish people
very patient with everyone
rather foolish herself at times
always cheerful, whatever happens

say: Talk about adding insult to injury. They lost my luggage and then charged me for the phone call.
options: A bad situation was made worse.
Someone was physically hurt at the airport.
A friend insulted him about his luggage.
The phone call turned out to be free.

say: Honestly, it's six of one and half a dozen of the other.
options: Both options are about the same.
One option is exactly twice as good.
There are six different options to choose from.
He would prefer to have a dozen of them.

say: Let's not split hairs. The gist is the same.
options: to stop arguing about tiny differences
to book a haircut before the meeting
to divide the work into equal parts
to start the whole discussion again
explain: Splitting hairs = focusing on trivial details.

say: She said nothing, but her silence spoke volumes.
options: Her silence revealed a lot.
She was busy reading a book.
She was speaking very loudly.
She simply had nothing to say.
explain: Speak volumes = communicate a lot without words.

say: A dragon who lends books for free? I'll believe it when I see it.
options: sceptical
delighted
frightened
convinced

say: The patient's improving, but we're not out of the woods yet.
options: There is still some danger.
They are lost somewhere in a forest.
The patient has already gone home.
Everything is perfect now, thankfully.
explain: Not out of the woods = still in difficulty.

say: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
options: revealed a secret
freed an animal
ruined the food
arrived too early
explain: Let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret.

say: Hardly a day goes by without some new scandal at the palace.
options: Scandals happen almost daily.
Scandals at the palace are very rare.
Life at the palace is quiet and calm.
The days at the palace pass quickly.
explain: Hardly a day without = nearly every day.

say: That's the last straw. I'm cancelling my membership.
options: This final problem has made him act.
He has run out of straws at the café.
He is about to join a new sports club.
He is very patient and will stay a member.
explain: The last straw = the final annoyance that causes action.

say: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise. It led me here.
options: Something bad turned out to be good.
She was blessed by a priest at her new job.
She wore a clever disguise to the interview.
She still deeply regrets losing that job.
